Recall the baby data from [Homework 5](/hw/hw-5.html#part-1-babies):

```{r}
#| message: false
births14 <- read_csv("data/births14.csv") |>
  filter(!is.na(habit))
```

We want to understand how reliably we can estimate the relationship between the mother's age in years (`mage`) and the birth weight in pounds of the baby (`weight`). You already did simulation-based inference. Now let's do inference using the bell curve.

::: callout-tip
## Reminder

The [in-class activity](/ae/ae-12-normal.html) from Tuesday introduced basic commands for working with the bell curve. You may find some of them useful today.
:::

## Setup

{{< include _setup.qmd >}}

## Task 1

Fit (and store!) the simple linear regression `weight ~ mage` using *both* techniques we have seen: the one involving `linear_reg` *and* the one involving `specify`. Display both sets of results and verify that they match.

## Task 2

Use the `filter` and `pull` commands to extract the point estimate and the **standard error** for the slope from the regression outputs in the previous part. Store these values in new variables `b1` and `SE`.

## Task 3

The central limit theorem (and other results) says that if our sample size is large enough, the **sampling distribution** of the regression slope can be approximated by $\text{N}(b_1,\,\text{SE})$. Based on this approximation and your numbers from the previous part, use the `qnorm` command to compute the lower bound and upper bound of a 90% confidence interval for the slope. 

## Task 4

Use `ggplot` together with the new layers `stat_function` and `geom_vline` to plot the normal distribution and the bounds of your confidence interval.

## Task 5 

Calculate, visualize, and interpret the $p$-value from a permutation test for the following hypotheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{H}_0&: \beta_1=0\\
\text{H}_A&: \beta_1\neq 0.
\end{aligned}
$$

So that we all get the same results, you should use the random number seed `123` and you should do `500` repititions of the simulation.

## Task 6

The central limit theorem (and other results) says that if our sample size is large enough, the **null distribution** of the regression slope can be approximated by $\text{N}(0,\,\text{SE})$. Let's use this approximation to re-do the test from the previous part.

a. Use the `normTail` command to visualize the $p$-value of the test;
a. Use the `pnorm` command to calculate the $p$-value of the test.
